rv.q: It gets gusts of laughter but can feel rather forced, and the joyous language is left to fend for itself.
I would have thought that crashing in and out of convention, underlining the risqué, would crush Wilde's celebrated witticisms. Actually, it releases them.
I loved it because it honours Wilde's wit but also his radicalism and his embrace of artifice.
You can't help but think Wilde would be wild about this production for its all-round misbehaviour, even if it does feel like subversion lite.
This is a big success, oh yes it is.

And things do not get noticeably straighter. On a set from Rae Smith that looks like a lysergically enhanced take on rep production cliche – the garden scene has a kind of Midsommar vibe – Algernon and his BFF Jack (Hugh Skinner) are played as gay men, as opposed to the usual ‘witty and English’.
Generally, the production is immensely enjoyable, delivered with irrepressible, infectious glee.
When it works, though, it's a joy.
But there's so much fizz and sparkle in the staging, and such charm, cheek and flair from the cast, that we're consistently tickled and ultimately won over.

Prior indications were that this would be memorably transgressive in approach, certainly a departure from the relatively staid Peter Hall National production of 1982, which boasted Judi Dench as Lady Bracknell, and was greeted by one critic as “unequivocally hetero”. Webster has talked about his intention to bring out “the queer shadow play”.
It's an utter delight, the perfect Christmas choice.
Fun, fabulous and fiery, it's a hoot.
There's no shortage of acid-tipped delight here to titillate and tantalise your sensibilities.
Webster's sparkling version brings out all the cutting observations of an Irish outsider looking in on the absurdities of English society.

Its bright colours and lavish costumes produce a suitably artificial reality like the flowers in the stage garden. Algy’s friend in the country, whose frequent illnesses provide an excuse for him to leave town, and Jack’s profligate younger brother, his excuse to come up to town, are inventions and the whole play is clever contrivance.
Joyfully directed and magnificently acted, this production should be prescribed as an effortless way to make even the biggest Grinch raise a smile.

cn.t: Critics praise Max Webster's flamboyantly camp, hot-pink production as joyous and exuberant, with most celebrating its bold foregrounding of Wilde's queer subtext, though a few find the over-the-top approach excessive.
